full_text:
Interviewer:	How are you enjoying your placement then?

Subject:	It’s mad. I’ve been up for 6½ hours already today

Interviewer:	So you’re ready for bed? OK, um, when did you start?

Subject:	I started my placement at the end of September, (20th?) September.

Interviewer:	Can you tell me about the company that you’re working for?

Subject:	The company that I work for is called [company], it’s one of the biggest charter companies in the UK and we provide flights basically on demand, both passenger and cargo. I work in the Cargo Department as a Flight Operations Manager, um, and we do post flights, we’ve worked for the royal family of Saudi Arabia, car parts, everything, if you need it moving, we do it.

Interviewer:	OK, how would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

Subject:	They have never had a female flight manager before, so I’m the first. And – we’re known as brokers? – there are no female brokers within the Cargo Department but there are a few in the Passenger Department. Um, they’re very aware that it’s a male-dominated world actually, and to be quite honest they’re quite male-dominated as well. So they’re learning, they’re learning still, with women.

Interviewer:	OK, we’ll talk a bit more about that later. Um, how useful do you think that your degree so far has been to the work you’re doing?

Subject:	Really really useful, it’s really relevant. Um, because I’m working in the air industry, so I’m doing management for aircraft as well, so yeah, it’s been really good.

Interviewer:	OK. Are there any particular skills that have been useful?

Subject:	Just generally, um, part of my course is, you know, aircraft knowledge and what it takes to run an airline, so that’s been quite helpful. Maybe some of the theory parts as to, you know, the psychology of transport, isn’t so helpful to us, but you know, the real practical parts have been quite good.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anything that you wish you had learned before you started the placement?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	OK, when you were at uni, were you taught about anything about health and safety?

Subject:	I had a health and safety brief before I left.

Interviewer:	Was that useful or relevant?

Subject:	Um, not really – well it was kind of a more general thing, you know, you have a specific one, a health and safety one when I joined the company, like, because I’m dealing with aircraft all the time, so it’s got to be pretty specific. Common sense really.
Interviewer:	OK, do you think that university could have done more to prepare you for the placement?

Subject:	Um, no, I don’t think so. I haven’t really thought about that. Um, no. I think it’s such a unique placement that you couldn’t prepare for it really, you just take it as you can. Um, yeah, they didn’t think I’d last at this job as long apparently, my company.

Interviewer:	Yeah? That’s interesting.

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Um, before you started the placement, did the university or your department say what they expected students to gain from going on placement?

Subject:	On this placement or…?

Interviewer:	Well, generally.

Subject:	Um, generally they expect us to come back a bit more mature, I think. We’ve had a bit of a taste of the world. Um, this placement, my department had really high expectations of us because they’ve taken a lot of [university] students and they say that we’re of a high standard so, um, they’d like us to do very well.

Interviewer:	OK. How have you found like the transition from education to work? 

Subject:	Easy. I’ve really enjoyed it, I haven’t found it that difficult. Um, coming back and seeing everyone doing their lectures and doing, oh I’ve got to write an essay for next, I’m like, ha ha. But I’ve got to be up at 4 o’clock in the morning so…

Interviewer:	OK. Have you had to face any new issues like…?

Subject:	Yes, sexual discrimination within the workplace.

Interviewer:	Like what sort of things?

Subject:	Men don’t – within this job, as a cargo manager, they don’t personally think that I can do it, and they don’t ever come to me first. If there’s a guy with me they’ll go to him, not me. And it takes a lot to get the fact that I can do a job just as well as my other placement student who’s there, you know, I think (inaudible).

Interviewer:	Were you expecting that sort of attitude before it started or…?

Subject:	Well I thought that it was very male-dominated but I thought I could handle it. It’s got me down a few times but I’ll just prove that, um, I’ve good enough for it. I’ve done it in the last week, I’ve been running my office, so there’s not a lot I can do other than get down and prove myself.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you feel that you do have to sort of work harder?

Subject:	Yeah I feel I have to work harder. I feel that when I make a mistake everyone’s just like, oh, you know, you didn’t know any better. There’s a guy working there with me, he started a month before me, he’s from [university] as well, um, I just found out he got a bonus in his pay packet for helping round the office in the first few weeks before I was there, but to be honest I don’t think I’ll get that. You know, he is an exceptionally good student but I think they rely on him a lot more than they would on me.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel that your educational experience reflects what it’s like in industry at all? Are they two totally different environments?

Subject:	I think my educational experience has been a lot of theory of how to run an airline. This is more the practical side. So although it is quite useful, my course, it’s not, you know, something that I can directly take the kind of situations from, every day’s new, so.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the benefit of doing the placement is that you can put the theoretical and practical side together…?

Subject:	You can fill in the bits that you’ve missed yes.

Interviewer:	… or do you think that the course could involve more practical…?

Subject:	No, I think, I think it’s a good balance. You know, I think I’m quite lucky in this placement because I know a lot of students will be just doing the theory as part of their placement so, I’m pretty lucky.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you feel about going back to uni when you finish the placement?

Subject:	I’m going to love it. I’m going to have weekends and go to bed at normal times. Yeah, I mean I’m looking forward to getting back to having a normal life for a while, but um, yeah, no I think it’ll probably motivate me, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, how would you say that work and university differ?

Subject:	In many many ways. I mean at the moment my job is basically my lifestyle, um, you know, I get up at 8 o’clock and I’m in the office until 10 or 11 o’clock at night. I fly two or three times a week. I live with the people that I work with. Um, you’ve just got no time for anything else, it takes over my life so it’s probably more than people who go in a 9 o’clock and finish at 5.30, then that’s it, so I think it’s quite a culture shock.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that university and work have different priorities and goals?

Subject:	University tends to be just about doing your essay and turning up to lectures, whereas this is me getting a flight out on … yeah there’s different importance on things, but I think it generally comes down to the job really. University’s always about, you know, your lectures and – whereas my job is flying planes, so.

Interviewer:	OK, does the company have a structure or programme in place for placement students to follow?

Subject:	Um, well the other male placement student has been given his booklet on what to do but I’m still waiting for mine.

Interviewer:	Right, OK.

Subject:	They do like us to go out and see all the different planes and we do a lot of (inaudible) work, so we go out and represent the planes and they like us to go and see as many planes as we can, you know, to know what the capabilities of the company are. But no, I’m still waiting for my booklet.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think it’s a good idea to have sort of a structure?

Subject:	Yeah, because then you don’t – you know, when I first joined it wasn’t very structured, my learning. I was basically flying two hours (inaudible) um, and I had to pick up the job on the go. I would rather someone sat me down – which is what happened to everyone else – and said, right, you’ve got to do this, this, this and this. You know, everyone else has had a handbook, and I’ve just been pushed out almost like …

Interviewer:	Have you discussed that with anybody then, the fact that they’ve had …?

Subject:	Um, I’ve discussed it with my boss in [town], my Operations Manager, um, but – I don’t know, really he says just like well that just the way it is sometimes, you know, um – but being thrown in at the deep end is quite a good way to learn this job. You’ve got to get out there, you’ve got to do it and you can’t rely on anyone else, so.

Interviewer:	OK. What exactly does your job role involve?

Subject:	OK, I work as a Flight Operations Manager. When a flight is sold in [town] by a broker and they then ring us up to say, we’re flying a plane on Tuesday (inaudible), um, we have a fleet of three aircraft and my airport, and then I plan the flight brief, I apply for flight plans, I sort out fuelling, handling, hotel arrangements, um, I sort out the flight funds, which is typically US $15,000, I think about €5,000. That’s my responsibility on any flight. Um, and just generally keep that flight running – and the office running. Um, so, you know, it’s planning a flight from start to finish.

Interviewer:	Sounds quite exciting.

Subject:	Hair-raising at times.

Interviewer:	Is that what you were expecting the job to be or what you were told to expect?

Subject:	Um yes, it was what I expected the job to be. Sometimes, you know, sometimes when the flight isn’t sold you don’t do anything for 2 or 3 days and then maybe 3 flights are sold in a day, so, that has its, you know, really really busy times, and you just want to cry. But …

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility?

Subject:	Yes, but I’d like a bit more compared to what [name], the other placement student, does. He has a lot more than me, and I think they rely on him, and I’d quite like them to actually realise that I can do the job as well. Um, so yes, sometimes it’s a bit much when everything is happening at once, but I can do it and I’d like to do more.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you feel like the company is supportive of you?

Subject:	Mm. Well, I found out on Friday that they’d took out a bet on how long I’d last in this job. No-one ever said this to my face, they said that I’d done really really well, but I think they have supported me but I don’t think they’re too sure about the whole women flight managers, so it’s my job to really prove that I, we can.

Interviewer:	So has that been people like colleagues or your superiors or people that are working for you that have had that, or everyone has had that attitude?

Subject:	Everyone I think. They are very – I didn’t realise how unusual it is to have a woman working in the cargo industry so it is, and I’ve really had to prove myself – but I’m getting there slowly.

Interviewer:	Good. Do you know if other women in the company have experienced …?

Subject:	 (inaudible) the only other two women are the secretaries.

Interviewer:	Do you get on with them?

Subject:	Er, yes, but you know, I very (inaudible) so I don’t really see them but, no-one does the kind of role that I do so I haven’t got anyone to compare myself to.

Interviewer:	OK, how would you summarise the placement experience so far?

Subject:	Um, it’s been absolutely fantastic. It’s been put down as the best placement you can do for my course, it’s been amazing – I’ve been places, seen things, that I wouldn’t have ever done. I’ve had the experiences and it’s making me grow up because I want to be in charge of a hell of a lot more than I did at university, so you know, one day I can be in the Sahara and the next day flying round England. It’s a great experience and (inaudible).

Interviewer:	OK, so what would you say have been the best and worst things about the placement so far?

Subject:	The best things? Probably flying in the Sahara Desert. That was pretty cool. The worst thing was – I don’t think – I just wish my company would think – I think they need to rely on me a bit more and treat me like I can do stuff. It may be that I haven’t given a good impression before, but I’m trying, really hard.

Interviewer:	OK, has the placement met your expectations?

Subject:	Yes, and more.

Interviewer:	Is there anything that you thought you would achieve but haven’t so far?

Subject:	No. I’m still in the middle of achieving just about everything, so …

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think that you’ve gained from the placement so far?

Subject:	A lot of experience of the airline industry, how it works, people’s attitudes, which you don’t get taught in the classroom. Um, (inaudible) responsibility, you know, it’s been good for me to grow up and have to organise myself, and get myself half way across the continent and back again. So it’s, you know, organisational abilities.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there’s any way that you could be taught about attitudes in the classroom, or is it just one of those things…?

Subject:	No, because I think sometimes the attitudes are in the classroom anyway, looking back on certain lecturers, it’s one of those things. 

Interviewer:	Is that something you think you don’t realise at the time, it’s only when you’re looking back?

Subject:	I thought it might just be a one-off, but it’s not, you know, it’s like any industry I guess. It’s just one of those sort of things.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there are any drawbacks at all to doing a placement? 

Subject:	To doing a placement? No. You can only really take positive things and it can help you decide what you want to do – like I don’t ever want to work in an office again, or, you know. I think it can be positive even if you don’t enjoy it that much.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think you’ll use what you’ve learned on placement when you come back to uni for your final year?

Subject:	I’ll probably end up doing a dissertation on something related to what I’m doing now, so I think it’s been, you know – we get to see how things are run and we’ve all got our own ideas on what we’d like to do, so I think really that’s going to help us.

Interviewer:	OK, you said that there’s another student on the placement and you’ve already told me a bit about this, but we’ll probably just discuss that a bit more, but do you think that you’re treated equally?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s because of your gender?

Subject:	Um … maybe 20% of it’s my gender. The other part is the fact he’s been there for a month longer than me, and also he is really good at his job, but I think they could let me do some of it. He does tend to – he’s very organised and he tends to take over doing something, so it frustrates me but he gets – he sometimes gets the, um, praise for doing it, he gets the recognition. 

Interviewer:	Was he on your course? 

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Did you know him before you started?

Subject:	Yeah, he used to go out with my best friend.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s been an advantage or disadvantage, having another student on placement? Or a bit of both?

Subject:	A bit of both, I mean he gets – it’s an advantage to me to see how he does something – when he does something he does it brilliantly, so you know, I can learn from him. But disadvantage in the fact that they do tend to rely on him, he’s the like more primary placement student and I, you know being a month after, starting a month after him, that’s been a disadvantage for me, but it was unavoidable, so.

Interviewer:	Do you support each other?

Subject:	Yes. Yeah, we’re first port of call for anything, you know, if we’ve got a problem then we go to each other first before anyone else. It’s easier for us to like put our ideas together and think about something rather than just going off (inaudible).You know, we try not to look like we don’t know what we’re doing. So far we’ve (inaudible).

Interviewer:	Have you discussed the issues about how you’re treated with each other, what does he think about it?

Subject:	It’s just one of those – I mean he’s really good so it’s not the fact that – you know, he does deserve everything he gets, but I would like a bit more.

Interviewer:	You deserve it too.

Subject:	I’d like a go, so yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that you’re treated the same as other permanent members of staff?

Subject:	I am a permanent member of staff, whereas everyone else is just temporary, which – 

Interviewer:	 (inaudible)

Subject:	Yeah, I’m treated pretty well.

Interviewer:	Do you have to do much group or team work?

Subject:	Yes, all day every day. I live with the people I work with, I mean it is just one big team effort because if one person does it, it’s just too much work, so we help each other out all the time.

Interviewer:	How do you think doing teamwork in the workplace compares to doing teamwork at uni?

Subject:	For us it’s a matter of (our job or not?), so we really do rely on each other, you know what each person is capable of doing within the job. Within the university, I don’t know, it still feels like you’re playing a bit, its still, oh XY and Z will do this and this, within work you just know straight away what person can achieve that and you tend to pick up on their strengths and weaknesses a bit better, I prefer it.

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s because when you’re at work the end result is a team effort whereas at university even though you’re … ?

Subject:	I think there’s more competitiveness with it. Yeah, I think, you know – but also in the workplace it’s your job on the line, if you’re not the one pulling your weight it’s going to show, whereas at uni you can generally cover it up. It shows a lot more.
Interviewer:	OK, are there any particular people that you’ve liked or disliked working with?

Subject:	Um, I quite like working with some of the brokers – you know, I work for the brokers in [town] so I get on quite well with them. Um, my financial director, I find him quite difficult to get on with sometimes.

Interviewer:	Any particular reasons?

Subject:	I really didn’t make too much of a good impression on him in the first week. Um, yeah – and our business is highly competitive and one of my friends rang me up just before I went flying and I said I’ve got to go, I’m going away, and he works within the same kind of industry and he found out and rang up and he said, oh I heard you’re plane’s going to X, Y, Z and my director was like, what, what did you tell him? And I was like, but I didn’t tell him, he found out, and basically I’ve got the blame and you know, they question my competence within the job just because of that one – which wasn’t even mine. So I’ve been working hard to make up for it since then.

Interviewer:	OK, have you been given a mentor in the company at all? Do you think it would be a good idea to have had one?

Subject:	On my first day I went in for like 4 or 5 hours and saw what they did, but that was the [town] side of it, it’s very different. Um, I’ve got my station manager, he tried, but – no, not really. Me and [name] kind of support each other.

Interviewer:	Is there anyone else that you’d go to for advice apart from [name]?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anyone in the company that you’d regard as like a role model at all?

Subject:	 [Name, placement student]. No, he’s fantastic, he really is, I mean he seems to know what to do instinctively so he’s the best role model, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, has anyone from university been to visit you yet?

Subject:	Yes, our placement tutor came out last week.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you know, why he came to see you, the purpose of it?

Subject:	Um, it was a social thing, they go and see every student. Um, so, it was just to check up everything’s going OK. He asked me how the job was going, and he apparently was very impressed.

Interviewer:	Did he speak to your supervisor?

Subject:	Yes he did. He had a quick chat with him.

Interviewer:	Did you know your placement tutor already?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	OK, have you discussed any of the sexist attitude stuff with him at all?

Subject:	We touched on it but, I don’t know, it’s not something that, you know, I feel really really affects me, but I can tell that it’s there. You know, I am a woman and the first thing anyone says is, oh, you’re a girl. So, you know, I can tell it’s there but I just put my head down and work through it. Sometimes it frustrates me, sometimes it works in my, works in my favour, like Russian crews won’t fly with a woman, they really don’t like me. So you know, sometimes it works against me, but other times the other crews will look after me as if I was one of their daughters, so you know, it’s six of one and half a dozen of the other. It’s just life really.

Interviewer:	OK, would you be happy to go to your placement tutor if you did have any problems at all? 

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Are you in contact with your placement tutor when they’re not coming to see you, do you email them or anything like that?

Subject:	Um, no, not really. If I’ve got some questions. But I haven’t, apart from saying when do you want the report written up by, but no.

Interviewer:	OK, do you know if there is a complaints procedure either at university or at the company if you did have any problems?

Subject:	I should imagine there is but until I have a complaint I’m not going to find out.

Interviewer:	OK, are there appropriate facilities for women in your organisation, like…?

Subject:	Yes, but I’ve been on a plane without a toilet before. The whole thing running around [name] airport trying to find one. But yeah, I work in an airport so.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Can you describe any particular occasions when you think that your gender has determined like reactions from colleagues or the outcome of particular events?

Subject:	Oh, well, just one thing that made me laugh is, um, on my first weekend in the job I had to work at [airport] and I had to get airside. I had my pass, but I asked one of my male friends to drive me and, um, the guy from the company came up and he said like, hi to my friend first and then me, and it turned out that my friend didn’t have a passport and they were kind of panicking, and like, whoa, what are we going to do, and I just felt like saying, well, it’s not him you need to worry about, I’m the one who’s doing the job here. Um, I just think it’s still so unusual to find women doing it, that men can’t really handle it. You know, the people that I come into contact with generally want to talk to men first, and me second.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that more women aren’t involved?

Subject:	I think it’s just a very unusual situation, you know, the only women you tend to find are secretaries, so people don’t know if - who I am, um, so it’s up to me to go out there and prove it, but you know, I’ve got my little badge, it says Flight Manager on it. So, you know, but they’re tending to recognise me more now, I even have a little website with planes spotters photos dedicated to us – I found that one out on Friday. No, they’re – yeah, they’re beginning to recognise what I can do, so.

Interviewer:	OK, do you still want a career in the air industry when you finish?

Subject:	Maybe. 

Interviewer:	Have you decided?

Subject:	Well chances are I’m going to be offered this job as part time next year, and possibly the year after that, so the option’s there and I’ve been offered a placement with a shipping company as well, when I finish, so I’ve got lots of options, it’s you know, 

(Interview interrupted by telephone call)

Interviewer:	Can’t work without you.

Subject:	He’s just a pain in the arse! He really is, he’s so bloody rude as well. He’s one of my – um, he was from [university] as well but he’s graduated and we took him on because we needed someone else, but he’s just so bloody rude.

Interviewer:	Do you think that your career ambitions have changed at all as a result of the placement?

Subject:	Um, yes. When I first got this placement I really felt quite lucky because we’re the highest paid placement, we were like yeah, look what we get to do. But now money doesn’t matter, it’s how I feel about the job. I couldn’t care if I got paid £8,000 a year but I was happy. £17,000 - you know, I don’t really get a social life apart from my workmates, but even then we’re never in the same place at the same time. Um, you certainly don’t get to form relationships. I mean my placement tutor said to me, how do you feel about doing this after (inaudible). I said well I sound a bit like a 15 year old but I want to like go out with someone and be in the same place at the same time for more than about 30 seconds. So I mean I want to have a life, eventually.

Interviewer:	OK, how have you found like living away and…?

Subject:	Fine.

Interviewer:	Yeah OK. Do you think that the placement experience will help you when you start work after you leave?

Subject:	I think I’ve got pretty much, um, unique kind of skills through this one, so either I’ll go straight back into kind of brokering for airlines or I might go back and do this job again, but yeah, I think it’s been a pretty good experience for me to have on my CV.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the placement experience will help you when you start work after graduation in terms of being in a male environment?

Subject:	Yes, it’s not going to be a shock. I think to some people on my course it might be, but I’ll have got used to it and I’ll know what to expect, so, yeah, I know that I’ve probably got to work harder just to prove myself.

Interviewer:	Yeah OK. Do you think that you would like to work for them when you graduate then?

Subject:	Maybe.

Interviewer:	You’re still undecided? Does it depend how the rest of the year goes?

Subject:	Yeah, I think it’s – yeah, it’s a very difficult job and … I don’t know, I’ll see. It’s something I’d like to do, definitely, um, but I think it’s going to be whether they want me to or whether I want to at the end of it. I might just get to the end of it and just say, oh I need a break, because I feel like I’ve been here for years and I’ve only been here 2½ months.

Interviewer:	OK, I asked you this question in the previous interview but I’m just going to see if it’s easier now that you’ve been working in the industry a while, and that is what five words would you now use to describe the culture and characteristics of the air industry?

Subject:	Male-dominated. Is that one or two?

Interviewer:	If you can’t find five that doesn’t matter.

Subject:	Male-dominated. Characteristics, um .. .very very dynamic. Um, not straightforward, just a complex, male-dominated, sexist, dynamic industry, which I can’t, yeah.

Interviewer:	And something else that you said earlier, it’s probably competitive as well.

Subject:	Yeah – very very competitive.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there are advantages to being a woman in a male-dominated field?

Subject:	Occasionally I get special treatment. Um, I think that when I do do something well it’s really noticed, you know, it really stands out. And people tend to remember me. But I don’t know, I think it’s, yeah, because it’s unusual, you do tend to stand out. I mean people are quite shocked at what I can and can’t do. So sometimes you know, like really simple things, they’re like, oh wow, you can do that, whereas its kind of a normal thing for other people.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that women should be encouraged or enabled to go into this sort of industry, or would your experiences … 

Subject:	Um, I think they’d really want to have to do it.

Interviewer:	Yeah?

Subject:	I don’t think it’s the real simple kind of job, it’s not easy for anyone. I think you’ve got to be a certain type of person to want to do this kind of job anyway. If they can, why not.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s everything. Thank you very much. That’s been helpful.

Um, they’re very aware that it’s a male-dominated world actually, and to be quite honest they’re quite male-dominated as well. So they’re learning, they’re learning still, with women.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, we’ll talk a bit more about that later. Um, how useful do you think that your degree so far has been to the work you’re doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Really really useful, it’s really relevant. Um, because I’m working in the air industry, so I’m doing management for aircraft as well, so yeah, it’s been really good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Are there any particular skills that have been useful?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Just generally, um, part of my course is, you know, aircraft knowledge and what it takes to run an airline, so that’s been quite helpful. Maybe some of the theory parts as to, you know, the psychology of transport, isn’t so helpful to us, but you know, the real practical parts have been quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is there anything that you wish you had learned before you started the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you were at uni, were you taught about anything about health and safety?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I had a health and safety brief before I left.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was that useful or relevant?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, not really – well it was kind of a more general thing, you know, you have a specific one, a health and safety one when I joined the company, like, because I’m dealing with aircraft all the time, so it’s got to be pretty specific. Common sense really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that university could have done more to prepare you for the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, no, I don’t think so. I haven’t really thought about that. Um, no. I think it’s such a unique placement that you couldn’t prepare for it really, you just take it as you can. Um, yeah, they didn’t think I’d last at this job as long apparently, my company.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah? That’s interesting.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Um, before you started the placement, did the university or your department say what they expected students to gain from going on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: On this placement or…?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Well, generally.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, generally they expect us to come back a bit more mature, I think. We’ve had a bit of a taste of the world. Um, this placement, my department had really high expectations of us because they’ve taken a lot of [university] students and they say that we’re of a high standard so, um, they’d like us to do very well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. How have you found like the transition from education to work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Easy. I’ve really enjoyed it, I haven’t found it that difficult. Um, coming back and seeing everyone doing their lectures and doing, oh I’ve got to write an essay for next, I’m like, ha ha. But I’ve got to be up at 4 o’clock in the morning so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you had to face any new issues like…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, sexual discrimination within the workplace.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Like what sort of things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Men don’t – within this job, as a cargo manager, they don’t personally think that I can do it, and they don’t ever come to me first. If there’s a guy with me they’ll go to him, not me. And it takes a lot to get the fact that I can do a job just as well as my other placement student who’s there, you know, I think (inaudible).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Were you expecting that sort of attitude before it started or…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well I thought that it was very male-dominated but I thought I could handle it. It’s got me down a few times but I’ll just prove that, um, I’ve good enough for it. I’ve done it in the last week, I’ve been running my office, so there’s not a lot I can do other than get down and prove myself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you feel that you do have to sort of work harder?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah I feel I have to work harder. I feel that when I make a mistake everyone’s just like, oh, you know, you didn’t know any better. There’s a guy working there with me, he started a month before me, he’s from [university] as well, um, I just found out he got a bonus in his pay packet for helping round the office in the first few weeks before I was there, but to be honest I don’t think I’ll get that. You know, he is an exceptionally good student but I think they rely on him a lot more than they would on me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you feel that your educational experience reflects what it’s like in industry at all? Are they two totally different environments?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think my educational experience has been a lot of theory of how to run an airline. This is more the practical side. So although it is quite useful, my course, it’s not, you know, something that I can directly take the kind of situations from, every day’s new, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the benefit of doing the placement is that you can put the theoretical and practical side together…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You can fill in the bits that you’ve missed yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: … or do you think that the course could involve more practical…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I think, I think it’s a good balance. You know, I think I’m quite lucky in this placement because I know a lot of students will be just doing the theory as part of their placement so, I’m pretty lucky.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you feel about going back to uni when you finish the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m going to love it. I’m going to have weekends and go to bed at normal times. Yeah, I mean I’m looking forward to getting back to having a normal life for a while, but um, yeah, no I think it’ll probably motivate me, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how would you say that work and university differ?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In many many ways. I mean at the moment my job is basically my lifestyle, um, you know, I get up at 8 o’clock and I’m in the office until 10 or 11 o’clock at night. I fly two or three times a week. I live with the people that I work with. Um, you’ve just got no time for anything else, it takes over my life so it’s probably more than people who go in a 9 o’clock and finish at 5.30, then that’s it, so I think it’s quite a culture shock.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that university and work have different priorities and goals?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: University tends to be just about doing your essay and turning up to lectures, whereas this is me getting a flight out on … yeah there’s different importance on things, but I think it generally comes down to the job really. University’s always about, you know, your lectures and – whereas my job is flying planes, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, does the company have a structure or programme in place for placement students to follow?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, well the other male placement student has been given his booklet on what to do but I’m still waiting for mine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Right, OK.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They do like us to go out and see all the different planes and we do a lot of (inaudible) work, so we go out and represent the planes and they like us to go and see as many planes as we can, you know, to know what the capabilities of the company are. But no, I’m still waiting for my booklet.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think it’s a good idea to have sort of a structure?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, because then you don’t – you know, when I first joined it wasn’t very structured, my learning. I was basically flying two hours (inaudible) um, and I had to pick up the job on the go. I would rather someone sat me down – which is what happened to everyone else – and said, right, you’ve got to do this, this, this and this. You know, everyone else has had a handbook, and I’ve just been pushed out almost like …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you discussed that with anybody then, the fact that they’ve had …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I’ve discussed it with my boss in [town], my Operations Manager, um, but – I don’t know, really he says just like well that just the way it is sometimes, you know, um – but being thrown in at the deep end is quite a good way to learn this job. You’ve got to get out there, you’ve got to do it and you can’t rely on anyone else, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What exactly does your job role involve?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: OK, I work as a Flight Operations Manager. When a flight is sold in [town] by a broker and they then ring us up to say, we’re flying a plane on Tuesday (inaudible), um, we have a fleet of three aircraft and my airport, and then I plan the flight brief, I apply for flight plans, I sort out fuelling, handling, hotel arrangements, um, I sort out the flight funds, which is typically US $15,000, I think about €5,000. That’s my responsibility on any flight. Um, and just generally keep that flight running – and the office running. Um, so, you know, it’s planning a flight from start to finish.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Sounds quite exciting.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hair-raising at times.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that what you were expecting the job to be or what you were told to expect?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um yes, it was what I expected the job to be. Sometimes, you know, sometimes when the flight isn’t sold you don’t do anything for 2 or 3 days and then maybe 3 flights are sold in a day, so, that has its, you know, really really busy times, and you just want to cry. But …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, but I’d like a bit more compared to what [name], the other placement student, does. He has a lot more than me, and I think they rely on him, and I’d quite like them to actually realise that I can do the job as well. Um, so yes, sometimes it’s a bit much when everything is happening at once, but I can do it and I’d like to do more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you feel like the company is supportive of you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm. Well, I found out on Friday that they’d took out a bet on how long I’d last in this job. No-one ever said this to my face, they said that I’d done really really well, but I think they have supported me but I don’t think they’re too sure about the whole women flight managers, so it’s my job to really prove that I, we can.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So has that been people like colleagues or your superiors or people that are working for you that have had that, or everyone has had that attitude?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Everyone I think. They are very – I didn’t realise how unusual it is to have a woman working in the cargo industry so it is, and I’ve really had to prove myself – but I’m getting there slowly.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Good. Do you know if other women in the company have experienced …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: (inaudible) the only other two women are the secretaries.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you get on with them?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yes, but you know, I very (inaudible) so I don’t really see them but, no-one does the kind of role that I do so I haven’t got anyone to compare myself to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how would you summarise the placement experience so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, it’s been absolutely fantastic. It’s been put down as the best placement you can do for my course, it’s been amazing – I’ve been places, seen things, that I wouldn’t have ever done. I’ve had the experiences and it’s making me grow up because I want to be in charge of a hell of a lot more than I did at university, so you know, one day I can be in the Sahara and the next day flying round England. It’s a great experience and (inaudible).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, so what would you say have been the best and worst things about the placement so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The best things? Probably flying in the Sahara Desert. That was pretty cool. The worst thing was – I don’t think – I just wish my company would think – I think they need to rely on me a bit more and treat me like I can do stuff. It may be that I haven’t given a good impression before, but I’m trying, really hard.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, has the placement met your expectations?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, and more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anything that you thought you would achieve but haven’t so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. I’m still in the middle of achieving just about everything, so …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think that you’ve gained from the placement so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: A lot of experience of the airline industry, how it works, people’s attitudes, which you don’t get taught in the classroom. Um, (inaudible) responsibility, you know, it’s been good for me to grow up and have to organise myself, and get myself half way across the continent and back again. So it’s, you know, organisational abilities.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that there’s any way that you could be taught about attitudes in the classroom, or is it just one of those things…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, because I think sometimes the attitudes are in the classroom anyway, looking back on certain lecturers, it’s one of those things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that something you think you don’t realise at the time, it’s only when you’re looking back?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I thought it might just be a one-off, but it’s not, you know, it’s like any industry I guess. It’s just one of those sort of things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that there are any drawbacks at all to doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: To doing a placement? No. You can only really take positive things and it can help you decide what you want to do – like I don’t ever want to work in an office again, or, you know. I think it can be positive even if you don’t enjoy it that much.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think you’ll use what you’ve learned on placement when you come back to uni for your final year?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’ll probably end up doing a dissertation on something related to what I’m doing now, so I think it’s been, you know – we get to see how things are run and we’ve all got our own ideas on what we’d like to do, so I think really that’s going to help us.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, you said that there’s another student on the placement and you’ve already told me a bit about this, but we’ll probably just discuss that a bit more, but do you think that you’re treated equally?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s because of your gender?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um … maybe 20% of it’s my gender. The other part is the fact he’s been there for a month longer than me, and also he is really good at his job, but I think they could let me do some of it. He does tend to – he’s very organised and he tends to take over doing something, so it frustrates me but he gets – he sometimes gets the, um, praise for doing it, he gets the recognition.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Was he on your course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you know him before you started?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, he used to go out with my best friend.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s been an advantage or disadvantage, having another student on placement? Or a bit of both?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: A bit of both, I mean he gets – it’s an advantage to me to see how he does something – when he does something he does it brilliantly, so you know, I can learn from him. But disadvantage in the fact that they do tend to rely on him, he’s the like more primary placement student and I, you know being a month after, starting a month after him, that’s been a disadvantage for me, but it was unavoidable, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you support each other?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Yeah, we’re first port of call for anything, you know, if we’ve got a problem then we go to each other first before anyone else. It’s easier for us to like put our ideas together and think about something rather than just going off (inaudible).You know, we try not to look like we don’t know what we’re doing. So far we’ve (inaudible).

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you discussed the issues about how you’re treated with each other, what does he think about it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s just one of those – I mean he’s really good so it’s not the fact that – you know, he does deserve everything he gets, but I would like a bit more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You deserve it too.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’d like a go, so yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that you’re treated the same as other permanent members of staff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I am a permanent member of staff, whereas everyone else is just temporary, which –

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: (inaudible)

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’m treated pretty well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have to do much group or team work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, all day every day. I live with the people I work with, I mean it is just one big team effort because if one person does it, it’s just too much work, so we help each other out all the time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you think doing teamwork in the workplace compares to doing teamwork at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: For us it’s a matter of (our job or not?), so we really do rely on each other, you know what each person is capable of doing within the job. Within the university, I don’t know, it still feels like you’re playing a bit, its still, oh XY and Z will do this and this, within work you just know straight away what person can achieve that and you tend to pick up on their strengths and weaknesses a bit better, I prefer it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s because when you’re at work the end result is a team effort whereas at university even though you’re … ?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think there’s more competitiveness with it. Yeah, I think, you know – but also in the workplace it’s your job on the line, if you’re not the one pulling your weight it’s going to show, whereas at uni you can generally cover it up. It shows a lot more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are there any particular people that you’ve liked or disliked working with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I quite like working with some of the brokers – you know, I work for the brokers in [town] so I get on quite well with them. Um, my financial director, I find him quite difficult to get on with sometimes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Any particular reasons?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I really didn’t make too much of a good impression on him in the first week. Um, yeah – and our business is highly competitive and one of my friends rang me up just before I went flying and I said I’ve got to go, I’m going away, and he works within the same kind of industry and he found out and rang up and he said, oh I heard you’re plane’s going to X, Y, Z and my director was like, what, what did you tell him? And I was like, but I didn’t tell him, he found out, and basically I’ve got the blame and you know, they question my competence within the job just because of that one – which wasn’t even mine. So I’ve been working hard to make up for it since then.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you been given a mentor in the company at all? Do you think it would be a good idea to have had one?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: On my first day I went in for like 4 or 5 hours and saw what they did, but that was the [town] side of it, it’s very different. Um, I’ve got my station manager, he tried, but – no, not really. Me and [name] kind of support each other.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is there anyone else that you’d go to for advice apart from [name]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is there anyone in the company that you’d regard as like a role model at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [Name, placement student]. No, he’s fantastic, he really is, I mean he seems to know what to do instinctively so he’s the best role model, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, has anyone from university been to visit you yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, our placement tutor came out last week.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you know, why he came to see you, the purpose of it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, it was a social thing, they go and see every student. Um, so, it was just to check up everything’s going OK. He asked me how the job was going, and he apparently was very impressed.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did he speak to your supervisor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes he did. He had a quick chat with him.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you know your placement tutor already?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you discussed any of the sexist attitude stuff with him at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We touched on it but, I don’t know, it’s not something that, you know, I feel really really affects me, but I can tell that it’s there. You know, I am a woman and the first thing anyone says is, oh, you’re a girl. So, you know, I can tell it’s there but I just put my head down and work through it. Sometimes it frustrates me, sometimes it works in my, works in my favour, like Russian crews won’t fly with a woman, they really don’t like me. So you know, sometimes it works against me, but other times the other crews will look after me as if I was one of their daughters, so you know, it’s six of one and half a dozen of the other. It’s just life really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, would you be happy to go to your placement tutor if you did have any problems at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you in contact with your placement tutor when they’re not coming to see you, do you email them or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, no, not really. If I’ve got some questions. But I haven’t, apart from saying when do you want the report written up by, but no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you know if there is a complaints procedure either at university or at the company if you did have any problems?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I should imagine there is but until I have a complaint I’m not going to find out.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, are there appropriate facilities for women in your organisation, like…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, but I’ve been on a plane without a toilet before. The whole thing running around [name] airport trying to find one. But yeah, I work in an airport so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Can you describe any particular occasions when you think that your gender has determined like reactions from colleagues or the outcome of particular events?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh, well, just one thing that made me laugh is, um, on my first weekend in the job I had to work at [airport] and I had to get airside. I had my pass, but I asked one of my male friends to drive me and, um, the guy from the company came up and he said like, hi to my friend first and then me, and it turned out that my friend didn’t have a passport and they were kind of panicking, and like, whoa, what are we going to do, and I just felt like saying, well, it’s not him you need to worry about, I’m the one who’s doing the job here. Um, I just think it’s still so unusual to find women doing it, that men can’t really handle it. You know, the people that I come into contact with generally want to talk to men first, and me second.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that more women aren’t involved?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s just a very unusual situation, you know, the only women you tend to find are secretaries, so people don’t know if - who I am, um, so it’s up to me to go out there and prove it, but you know, I’ve got my little badge, it says Flight Manager on it. So, you know, but they’re tending to recognise me more now, I even have a little website with planes spotters photos dedicated to us – I found that one out on Friday. No, they’re – yeah, they’re beginning to recognise what I can do, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you still want a career in the air industry when you finish?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Maybe.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you decided?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well chances are I’m going to be offered this job as part time next year, and possibly the year after that, so the option’s there and I’ve been offered a placement with a shipping company as well, when I finish, so I’ve got lots of options, it’s you know, (Interview interrupted by telephone call)

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Can’t work without you.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: He’s just a pain in the arse! He really is, he’s so bloody rude as well. He’s one of my – um, he was from [university] as well but he’s graduated and we took him on because we needed someone else, but he’s just so bloody rude.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that your career ambitions have changed at all as a result of the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, yes. When I first got this placement I really felt quite lucky because we’re the highest paid placement, we were like yeah, look what we get to do. But now money doesn’t matter, it’s how I feel about the job. I couldn’t care if I got paid £8,000 a year but I was happy. £17,000 - you know, I don’t really get a social life apart from my workmates, but even then we’re never in the same place at the same time. Um, you certainly don’t get to form relationships. I mean my placement tutor said to me, how do you feel about doing this after (inaudible). I said well I sound a bit like a 15 year old but I want to like go out with someone and be in the same place at the same time for more than about 30 seconds. So I mean I want to have a life, eventually.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how have you found like living away and…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Fine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah OK. Do you think that the placement experience will help you when you start work after you leave?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think I’ve got pretty much, um, unique kind of skills through this one, so either I’ll go straight back into kind of brokering for airlines or I might go back and do this job again, but yeah, I think it’s been a pretty good experience for me to have on my CV.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the placement experience will help you when you start work after graduation in terms of being in a male environment?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, it’s not going to be a shock. I think to some people on my course it might be, but I’ll have got used to it and I’ll know what to expect, so, yeah, I know that I’ve probably got to work harder just to prove myself.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah OK. Do you think that you would like to work for them when you graduate then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Maybe.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’re still undecided? Does it depend how the rest of the year goes?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think it’s – yeah, it’s a very difficult job and … I don’t know, I’ll see. It’s something I’d like to do, definitely, um, but I think it’s going to be whether they want me to or whether I want to at the end of it. I might just get to the end of it and just say, oh I need a break, because I feel like I’ve been here for years and I’ve only been here 2½ months.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, I asked you this question in the previous interview but I’m just going to see if it’s easier now that you’ve been working in the industry a while, and that is what five words would you now use to describe the culture and characteristics of the air industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Male-dominated. Is that one or two?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: If you can’t find five that doesn’t matter.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Male-dominated. Characteristics, um .. .very very dynamic. Um, not straightforward, just a complex, male-dominated, sexist, dynamic industry, which I can’t, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And something else that you said earlier, it’s probably competitive as well.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah – very very competitive.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that there are advantages to being a woman in a male-dominated field?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Occasionally I get special treatment. Um, I think that when I do do something well it’s really noticed, you know, it really stands out. And people tend to remember me. But I don’t know, I think it’s, yeah, because it’s unusual, you do tend to stand out. I mean people are quite shocked at what I can and can’t do. So sometimes you know, like really simple things, they’re like, oh wow, you can do that, whereas its kind of a normal thing for other people.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that women should be encouraged or enabled to go into this sort of industry, or would your experiences …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I think they’d really want to have to do it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t think it’s the real simple kind of job, it’s not easy for anyone. I think you’ve got to be a certain type of person to want to do this kind of job anyway. If they can, why not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s everything. Thank you very much. That’s been helpful.
